processing: A gongfu black tea of the Sichuan type: withered, rolled, oxidised, dried and refined. Since the 1970s, Sichuan makers have largely moved from sun-and-charcoal handwork to heated withering, rolling machines and dryers.
harvest_season: Very early spring; Sichuan black tea from this south-eastern area can reach the market around April. Spring leaf has a noticeably different aroma from summer and autumn pickings.
appearance_dry: Plump, round, tight strips, glossy black.
appearance_wet: Thick, soft leaf of an even red.
taste_profile: Fresh, clean aroma and a mellow, full, lively cup; Sichuan gongfu black teas as a group are known for a note of orange and candy.

brewing.notes: Short early steeps keep the citrus-sweet aroma clear. For a mug, about 3 g in 250 ml for 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year tea, and its whole point is earliness, so the new spring lot is what to look for. Drink it within a year or two. It is not an ageing tea; older stock simply loses its fresh aroma.
description:
Zao Bai Jian is the best-known black tea of Junlian and the wider Yibin area in south-eastern Sichuan. The name, roughly early white tip, belongs both to a local tea variety and to the gongfu tea made from it, a prized member of the Sichuan black tea family, Chuan Hong.

The bushes bud early, and the tea's reputation rests on that. Local shorthand describes it as early, tender, quick and good. It follows the usual gongfu sequence, with modern lines having replaced most of the old handwork.

Expect a fresh aroma and a mellow, full cup, and in good lots the orange-and-candy note associated with Sichuan gongfu teas. Use short steeps at first; long ones blur the aroma.

Buy the newest spring lot you can find, and ask who made it. Zao Bai Jian is also a company and brand name, so judge by the tea.

If you enjoy it, try it next to Qimen and Dian Hong, the two gongfu teas Chuan Hong is usually compared with.
history:
Sichuan gongfu black tea dates from the 1950s, when Junlian's gongfu tea was first exported to the Soviet Union. The Zao Bai Jian line grew from that export trade, and its early arrival on the international market was a real advantage.

Junlian gongfu Zao Bai Jian is recorded as taking a gold medal at a world food fair in Lisbon in 1985, followed by another for its broken tea at Geneva in 1986. The Chuan Hong trade took a hard hit in the 1990s as markets changed, and the making of Chuan Hong was listed as Sichuan intangible heritage in 2014.
